result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.simplify()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Remove all self-loops and duplicate edges, making the graph simple. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L2291-L2402){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.simplify() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Simplify](/assets/graphs/simplify.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Before: a four-node cycle with a self-loop on B and a second, parallel edge between C and D, both in the accent color. After simplify(), the self-loop and the duplicate edge are gone, shown dashed, leaving a simple four-node cycle." width="100%"} A simple graph has no self-loops (edges from a node to itself) and no multi-edges (multiple edges between the same pair of nodes). This method removes both types, which is a common preprocessing step for algorithms that require simple graphs. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} `simplify()` is exactly `remove_selfloops()` followed by `remove_duplicate_edges()` rolled into one call: self-loops disappear and each group of parallel edges collapses to its earliest survivor (lowest edge ID). Directedness affects only the second step, since $(u, v)$ and $(v, u)$ are distinct pairs in a directed graph but the same pair when undirected. Once it returns, `is_simple()` is guaranteed to be `True`, which is the condition many algorithms in the library quietly assume. ## Examples {.doc-examples} `simplify()` combines `remove_selfloops()` and `remove_duplicate_edges()` in one call. This graph starts with a duplicate "A"-"B" edge and two self-loops, so it isn't simple: ::: {#a5194367 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ( ec.Graph() .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_edge(source="A", target="B", weight=1.0) .add_edge(source="A", target="B", weight=2.0) # duplicate .add_edge(source="A", target="A") # self-loop .add_edge(source="B", target="B") # self-loop ) g.count_edges(), g.is_simple() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (4, False) ``` ::: ::: After simplifying, only the single genuine "A"-"B" edge remains, and `is_simple()` confirms it: ::: {#db86f4cd .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ( ec.Graph() .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_edge(source="A", target="B", weight=1.0) .add_edge(source="A", target="B", weight=2.0) .add_edge(source="A", target="A") .add_edge(source="B", target="B") .simplify() ) g.count_edges(), g.is_simple() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (1, True) ``` ::: ::: This makes `simplify()` a convenient one-line preprocessing step whenever an algorithm requires a simple graph: ::: {#e937b1f4 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ( ec.Graph() .add_node(label="X") .add_node(label="Y") .add_node(label="Z") .add_edge(source="X", target="Y") .add_edge(source="X", target="Y") # duplicate .add_edge(source="Y", target="Z") .add_edge(source="Z", target="Z") # self-loop .simplify() ) g.is_simple() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` True ``` ::: :::
